hero.label: MongoDB Operators
hero.heading: MongoDB Operators & BSON Types
hero.text: A complete reference for MongoDB BSON Data Types and all major Query Operators — Comparison, Logical, Element, Evaluation, Array, and Update operators — with real examples, use cases, and interview Q&A.

parts: BSON (Binary JSON) is the internal storage format used by MongoDB. It extends JSON with additional data types like
, and
. Every field value in a MongoDB document has a BSON type.

items.definition: Stores UTF-8 text. Most common BSON type. Used for names, emails, descriptions. Example: "firstName": "Shivam"
Stores integers or floating-point numbers. Int32 for small numbers, Int64 for large, Double for decimals. Example: "age": 25, "price": 99.99
Stores true or false. Used for status flags, toggles, feature flags. Example: "isActive": true, "isDeleted": false
Stores date and time as milliseconds since Unix epoch. Used for timestamps. Example: "createdAt": ISODate("2025-06-19T10:00:00Z")
12-byte unique identifier auto-generated for every document as _id. Contains timestamp, machine id, process id, and random counter. Example: "_id": ObjectId("66abc123...")
Stores an ordered list of values. Elements can be of any BSON type including nested documents. Example: "skills": ["Node.js", "MongoDB", "TypeScript"]
Stores nested documents as field values. Perfect for grouped data like address or profile. Example: "address": { "city": "Delhi", "pin": "110001" }
Represents an explicitly absent or undefined value. Different from a missing field. Example: "middleName": null
High-precision decimal type for financial and scientific calculations where floating-point rounding errors are unacceptable. Example: "price": NumberDecimal("99.9999")
Stores raw binary data such as images, files, encrypted content, UUIDs. Example: "profilePicture": BinData(0, "...base64...")

parts: Comparison operators are used inside a
filter to compare a field value against a given value. They always appear inside a field object like

items.definition: Matches documents where the field equals the specified value. Equivalent to writing { field: value } directly. Explicit form: { age: { $eq: 25 } }
Matches documents where the field does NOT equal the value. Useful for excluding a specific value. Example: find all users who are not admins.
Matches documents where the field value is strictly greater than the given value. Example: age > 18.
Matches documents where the field value is greater than or equal to the given value. Example: age >= 18 (includes 18).
Matches documents where the field value is strictly less than the given value. Example: price < 1000.
Matches documents where the field value is less than or equal to the given value. Example: price <= 1000 (includes 1000).
Matches documents where the field value equals any value in the provided array. Much more efficient than multiple $or conditions. Example: role is admin OR manager OR superadmin.
Matches documents where the field value does NOT equal any value in the provided array. Opposite of $in. Example: exclude guests and banned users.

parts: Logical operators combine multiple conditions. They accept an array of condition objects.
and
are the most common.
is the NOR (none of these), and
negates a single condition.

items.definition: Joins two or more conditions with AND logic. ALL conditions must be true for a document to match. MongoDB implicitly applies $and when you list multiple fields in a filter object, but explicit $and is needed when the same field appears in multiple conditions.
Joins two or more conditions with OR logic. At least ONE condition must be true. Commonly used to search across multiple fields or match multiple possible values.
Opposite of $or. Matches documents where NONE of the conditions are true. Useful for strict exclusion logic where you want to exclude multiple groups at once.
Inverts a single condition applied to a field. Takes an expression object (not an array). Matches documents where the field does NOT satisfy the given condition OR the field does not exist.

parts: Element operators check properties of a field itself rather than its value — whether the field
in the document, or what
its value is.

items.definition: Matches documents where the specified field exists (true) or does not exist (false). A field set to null still 'exists' — $exists: true matches it. Use $exists: false to find documents that are completely missing a field.

Matches documents where the specified field's value is of a particular BSON type. You can pass the type name as a string ("string", "number", "bool", "date", "objectId", "array", "null") or the BSON type number (e.g., 2 for String, 16 for Int32).

parts: Evaluation operators evaluate expressions or content within a field. The most used are
for pattern matching and
for full-text search. Others like
allow aggregation expressions in queries.

items.definition: Matches documents where the field value matches a given regular expression pattern. Supports flags: i (case-insensitive), m (multiline), x (extended). Use carefully on large collections — it cannot use standard indexes efficiently unless anchored at the start (^pattern).

Performs full-text search on fields that have a text index. Much more efficient than $regex for large-scale search. Supports language-specific stemming and stop words. Requires a text index to be created first on the collection.
Allows using aggregation pipeline expressions inside a find() query filter. Useful for comparing two fields within the same document, or applying computed logic in a filter.
Allows running JavaScript expressions as a query filter. Deprecated and very slow — avoids collection index usage entirely. Never use in production. $expr is the modern replacement.

parts: Array operators are used to query documents with array fields.
checks that all values exist in the array,
checks the array length, and
applies multiple conditions to a single array element.

items.definition: Matches documents where the array field contains ALL of the specified values (in any order). If any value is missing, the document is excluded. Example: find users who have BOTH Node.js AND MongoDB skills.
Matches documents where the array field has exactly the specified number of elements. Does not accept ranges ($gt, $lt). To query ranges of array sizes, use $where or check array index existence.

Matches documents where at least one array element satisfies ALL the given conditions simultaneously. Without $elemMatch, each condition can be satisfied by a different element. Use $elemMatch when elements are objects with multiple fields.

parts: Update operators are used inside
, or
to modify field values. They are always placed inside an object passed as the second argument.

items.definition: Sets the value of a specific field. If the field does not exist, it is created. Leaves all other fields untouched. This is the most used update operator — always prefer $set over direct replacement.
Removes a field from the document entirely. The value provided does not matter — use empty string by convention. Example: $unset: { temporaryToken: "" }
Increments a numeric field by a given amount. Use a negative value to decrement. Atomic — safe for concurrent operations like counters, view counts, stock quantities.
Multiplies the value of a numeric field by a given factor. Useful for applying percentage changes or scaling values.
Renames a field to a new name. The value is preserved. Useful during schema migrations or refactoring.

items.term: $min — Set if New Value is Less
items.definition: Updates the field only if the provided value is less than the current value. Useful for tracking minimums like lowest price, earliest date.

items.term: $max — Set if New Value is Greater
items.definition: Updates the field only if the provided value is greater than the current value. Useful for tracking maximums like highest score, latest timestamp.
Sets the value of a field to the current date or timestamp. Accepts { $type: 'date' } or { $type: 'timestamp' }.

parts: These operators modify array fields inside documents. Use
to add elements,
to remove specific elements,
to remove from the ends, and
to add only if the value does not already exist.

items.definition: Appends one or more elements to an array field. If the field does not exist, it is created as an array. Use with $each to push multiple elements at once. Use with $position to insert at a specific index.
Removes all elements from an array that match a specified value or condition. Can remove by exact value or by a query condition using operators like $gt, $in.
Adds an element to an array only if it does not already exist. Prevents duplicate values automatically. Ideal for tags, categories, watchlists — any set-like array.
Removes the first (-1) or last (1) element of an array. Does not target by value — only by position.
Removes all occurrences of all specified values from the array at once. Unlike $pull, it does not accept query operators — only exact values.
Used with $push or $addToSet to insert multiple elements in a single operation instead of calling the operator repeatedly.
Used with $push and $each to limit the array to a maximum number of elements after pushing. Positive = keep from start, Negative = keep from end.

parts: Projection controls which fields are returned in query results. Pass a projection object as the second argument to
. Use
to include a field and
to exclude it. You cannot mix include and exclude in the same projection (except for
which can always be excluded).

items.definition: Return only the specified fields. All other fields are excluded. Example: { name: 1, email: 1 } returns only name and email (_id included by default).
Return all fields EXCEPT the specified ones. Example: { password: 0, __v: 0 } returns everything except password and __v.
_id is always included by default even in inclusion projections. Explicitly set { _id: 0 } to remove it from results.
Returns only the first array element that matches the condition, rather than the entire array.
Returns a specified number of elements from an array — first N, last N, or a range.

rows: None of conditions can be true
Update if new value is smaller
Update if new value is larger

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Never use update without $set — without it MongoDB replaces the ENTIRE document with only the fields you sent. Always wrap updates in { $set: { ... } }.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Use $addToSet instead of $push when adding to arrays where duplicates are not allowed — like tags, skills, or roles. It checks uniqueness automatically.

blocks.title: Warning
blocks.text: $regex is slow on large collections unless the pattern is anchored at the start (^pattern) and the field is indexed. For full-text search use a text index with $text instead.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: $exists: false and { field: null } are different. $exists: false only matches documents where the field is completely absent. { field: null } matches both absent fields AND fields explicitly set to null.

blocks.title: Short Answer
blocks.text: Comparison: $gt $lt $in. Logical: $and $or $nor $not. Element: $exists $type. Evaluation: $regex $text $expr. Array: $all $size $elemMatch. Update: $set $inc $push $pull $addToSet.

blocks.title: Interview
blocks.text: What is the difference between $or and $in? — $in checks ONE field against multiple values. $or can check DIFFERENT fields with different conditions. { role: { $in: ["a","b"] } } is more efficient than { $or: [{role:"a"},{role:"b"}] } for the same field.

rows: Find users who are not guests
Find users with role admin OR manager
Find users that are NOT admin or manager
Update one field without touching others

items.title: What is the difference between $or and $in?
items.text: $in checks ONE field against an array of values — { role: { $in: ["admin","manager"] } }. $or checks MULTIPLE fields or conditions — { $or: [{role:"admin"},{age:{$gt:30}}] }. When checking the same field against multiple values, $in is more efficient and readable than $or.

items.title: What is the difference between $pull and $pop?
items.text: $pull removes elements by VALUE or condition — { $pull: { skills: "PHP" } } removes all occurrences of "PHP". $pop removes by POSITION — $pop: { arr: 1 } removes the last element, $pop: { arr: -1 } removes the first. Use $pull when you know the value, $pop when you need to trim the ends.

items.title: What is the difference between $push and $addToSet?
items.text: $push always adds the element to the array, even if it already exists — it allows duplicates. $addToSet adds the element ONLY if it is not already present — it enforces uniqueness. Use $addToSet for tags, roles, or skills where duplicates make no sense.

items.title: When should you use $elemMatch vs dot notation?
items.text: Use $elemMatch when querying arrays of objects where multiple conditions must apply to the SAME element. With dot notation, each condition can be satisfied by different elements in the array, which can cause false positives. Example: { scores: { $elemMatch: { subject: "Math", score: { $gt: 90 } } } } ensures the same score object satisfies both conditions.

items.title: What is the difference between $text and $regex for search?
items.text: $regex does character-level pattern matching and is flexible but slow on large collections unless anchored with ^. $text uses a pre-built text index and is much faster for keyword search — it supports stemming, stop words, and language awareness. Use $regex for specific pattern matching, use $text for full-text keyword search at scale.

items.title: What does $expr allow that regular operators cannot?
items.text: $expr allows you to compare two fields within the SAME document in a query filter. Example: find orders where discount > tax — { $expr: { $gt: ["$discount", "$tax"] } }. Regular comparison operators can only compare a field to a literal value, not to another field.

items.question: What is the difference between $gt and $gte?
items.answer: $gt is strictly greater than — it excludes the boundary value. $gte is greater than or equal — it includes the boundary value. Example: $gt: 18 matches 19, 20, 21 but NOT 18. $gte: 18 matches 18, 19, 20, 21.

items.question: Why is $in preferred over $or when checking one field against multiple values?
items.answer: Both produce the same result but $in is more readable and slightly more efficient because MongoDB can optimize a single field check against an array better than parsing multiple $or branches. { role: { $in: ["admin","manager"] } } is cleaner than { $or: [{role:"admin"},{role:"manager"}] }.

items.question: What is the difference between $exists: false and checking for null?
items.answer: $exists: false matches documents where the field is completely absent — it does not exist in the document at all. { field: null } matches documents where the field is absent OR is explicitly set to null. They behave differently for documents that have { middleName: null } — null query matches it, $exists: false does not.

items.question: What is the difference between $not and $nor?
items.answer: $not applies to a single field and negates one condition — { age: { $not: { $lt: 18 } } }. $nor applies at the top level and accepts an array of conditions — all conditions must be false for a document to match. $nor is like a negated $or.

items.question: Why is $regex slow and how do you make it faster?
items.answer: $regex cannot fully use standard B-tree indexes unless the pattern is anchored at the start with ^ (prefix match). For full-text search on large collections, create a text index and use $text which is significantly faster and supports language-aware matching. Use $regex only for specific pattern needs like email format validation queries.

items.question: What happens if you use update without $set?
items.answer: Without $set, MongoDB replaces the entire document with only the fields you provided. If you call updateOne({ _id: id }, { age: 25 }) the resulting document will only have { _id, age: 25 } — all other fields are deleted. Always use { $set: { age: 25 } } to update specific fields while preserving the rest.

items.question: What is the difference between Decimal128 and Double in BSON?
items.answer: Double is a standard IEEE 754 64-bit floating-point number — it has rounding errors for very precise decimal values. Decimal128 is a 128-bit high-precision decimal type that avoids rounding errors. Use Decimal128 for financial amounts, scientific calculations, or anywhere decimal precision is critical.

items.question: [Medium] How does MongoDB handle the $and operator implicitly vs explicitly?
items.answer: When you write multiple fields in a filter object — { age: { $gt: 18 }, isActive: true } — MongoDB automatically applies an implicit $and. The explicit $and array syntax — { $and: [ {age:{$gt:18}}, {age:{$lt:60}} ] } — is required when you need to apply multiple conditions to the SAME field, because a plain JS object cannot have duplicate keys. In all other cases, implicit $and is cleaner.

items.question: [Medium] What is $elemMatch and why is dot notation not always sufficient for array queries?
items.answer: When querying arrays of objects with multiple conditions, dot notation checks each condition independently across different array elements. { 'scores.subject': 'Math', 'scores.score': { $gte: 90 } } matches a document where one element has subject 'Math' and ANY other element has score >= 90. $elemMatch — { scores: { $elemMatch: { subject: 'Math', score: { $gte: 90 } } } } — ensures BOTH conditions apply to the SAME single element. This distinction is critical for correctness in nested array queries.

items.question: [Medium] What is the difference between updateOne() returning a result object vs findByIdAndUpdate() returning a document?
items.answer: updateOne() and updateMany() return a write result object: { acknowledged, matchedCount, modifiedCount, upsertedId }. They do NOT return the modified document. findByIdAndUpdate() and findOneAndUpdate() return the actual document — old version by default, or updated version when { new: true } is passed. Choose updateOne() for fire-and-forget updates, findByIdAndUpdate() when you need to return the document to the client.

items.question: [Medium] Explain how $expr enables comparing two fields inside the same document.
items.answer: $expr allows using aggregation pipeline expressions inside a find() query filter. Without $expr you cannot compare two fields of the same document — operators only compare a field to a literal. Example: find products where discountedPrice is less than originalPrice — db.products.find({ $expr: { $lt: ['$discountedPrice', '$originalPrice'] } }). The dollar-prefixed strings refer to the document's own field values.

items.question: [Medium] What is the difference between $pull and $pullAll?
items.answer: $pull removes elements from an array that match a specified VALUE or CONDITION — it accepts query operators like $gt, $in. { $pull: { scores: { $lt: 50 } } } removes all scores below 50. $pullAll removes all occurrences of each value in a provided array of EXACT values — no operators allowed. { $pullAll: { skills: ['PHP','jQuery'] } } removes both. Use $pull for conditional removal, $pullAll for bulk exact-value removal.

items.question: [Medium] How does the $slice update modifier work with $push?
items.answer: $slice is a modifier used inside $push with $each to limit the final size of an array after inserting. It accepts a positive number (keep from start), negative number (keep from end), or zero (empty the array). Example — maintain a notifications array capped at 10 latest entries: { $push: { notifications: { $each: [newNotif], $slice: -10 } } }. This is an atomic operation — the push and trim happen in one database call.

items.question: [Medium] What is the practical difference between $text full-text search and $regex?
items.answer: $regex does character-level pattern matching — it scans each character of field values. It cannot use B-tree indexes unless anchored with ^ at the start. For case-insensitive searches it always requires a collection scan. $text uses a pre-built inverted text index — extremely fast for keyword search, supports language stemming (run/running/ran all match 'run'), stop words, phrase search with quotes, and word exclusion with minus. $regex is best for format validation, $text for keyword-based search at scale.

items.question: [Medium] What does { $type: 'null' } match vs { $exists: false }?
items.answer: { field: { $type: 'null' } } matches documents where the field exists AND is explicitly set to null. { field: { $exists: false } } matches documents where the field is completely absent from the document. A document with { middleName: null } is matched by $type: 'null' but NOT by $exists: false. A document with no middleName field at all is matched by $exists: false but NOT by $type: 'null'. These are three distinct states: missing field, null value, or actual value.

items.question: [Advanced] How would you design a query to find users who have ALL required skills AND at least one preferred skill?
items.answer: Use $and combining $all (for required skills) and $in (for preferred skills) on the same skills array field. Since both conditions target the same field, explicit $and is needed: db.users.find({ $and: [ { skills: { $all: ['Node.js', 'MongoDB'] } }, { skills: { $in: ['TypeScript', 'Docker', 'AWS'] } } ] }). This returns users who definitely have Node.js AND MongoDB, and also have at least one of TypeScript, Docker, or AWS. Without explicit $and, you cannot apply both $all and $in to the same field key in one object.

items.question: [Advanced] How would you atomically increment a counter and cap an array in one MongoDB operation?
items.answer: MongoDB allows multiple update operators in a single updateOne() call as long as they target different fields. Combine $inc for the counter and $push with $each + $slice for the capped array: db.posts.updateOne({ _id: postId }, { $inc: { commentCount: 1 }, $push: { recentComments: { $each: [newComment], $slice: -5 } } }). This atomically increments the counter AND appends the new comment while keeping only the 5 most recent — all in one network round-trip and one atomic write.

items.question: [Advanced] Explain how $nor differs from combining $not with $or, and when you would choose each.
items.answer: $nor: [A, B, C] matches documents where NONE of the conditions A, B, or C are true — equivalent to NOT(A OR B OR C). You could rewrite it as { $not: { $or: [A, B, C] } } but $not cannot wrap top-level logical operators directly — it only works on field expressions. So $nor is the correct way to express 'none of these conditions'. Use $nor when you want to exclude multiple independent groups at once: { $nor: [{ role: 'guest' }, { isActive: false }, { isDeleted: true }] } returns only documents that are not guests, are active, and are not deleted.

items.question: [Advanced] How do you perform a case-insensitive partial text search efficiently on a large collection?
items.answer: There are three approaches with different trade-offs. 1) $regex with i flag — simple but performs a full collection scan, O(n). Acceptable only for small collections or admin-only endpoints. 2) Prefix-anchored $regex (^pattern) — can use a B-tree index but only for prefix matches, not contains. 3) $text with text index — create db.articles.createIndex({ title: 'text', content: 'text' }) then use { $text: { $search: 'keyword' } }. This is fastest for keyword search, supports language stemming, but does not support partial contains or regex patterns. For a production autocomplete, consider Atlas Search (Lucene-based) which combines speed with fuzzy matching.

items.question: [Advanced] How would you update only array elements matching a condition using the positional $ operator?
items.answer: MongoDB's positional $ operator references the first matching array element found by the query filter. It is used in the update to modify that specific element without knowing its index. Example — mark the first 'pending' order item as 'shipped': db.orders.updateOne({ _id: orderId, 'items.status': 'pending' }, { $set: { 'items.$.status': 'shipped', 'items.$.shippedAt': new Date() } }). The $ in the update path refers to the index of the element that matched 'items.status': 'pending' in the query. To update ALL matching elements use $[] (all elements) or $[identifier] with arrayFilters for conditional bulk updates.

items.question: [Advanced] What is the difference between $min/$max update operators and using $set with a conditional in application code?
items.answer: $min and $max are atomic server-side operations — they compare and update in a single round-trip with no race condition. If you use application code (fetch value, compare in JS, then $set), there is a window between the read and write where another process can change the value — a classic race condition in concurrent systems. $min: { lowestPrice: 499 } guarantees that the update only happens if 499 is truly less than the current value at the moment of write. This is critical for tracking minimum/maximum values in high-concurrency scenarios like auction lowest bids or inventory price floors.

items.question: Can I combine multiple operators in one query?
items.answer: Yes. MongoDB query operators compose naturally. Example: find active adults with admin or manager role — db.users.find({ isActive: true, age: { $gte: 18 }, role: { $in: ['admin','manager'] } }). You can nest $and, $or, $nor inside each other for complex logic.

items.question: What is the difference between $pullAll and $pull?
items.answer: $pull removes elements matching a value or a query condition — it accepts operators like $gt, $in. $pullAll removes all occurrences of each specified exact value in a single call. Use $pullAll for removing multiple known values at once, $pull when you need condition-based removal.

items.question: Does $addToSet work with arrays of objects?
items.answer: Yes, but it checks for deep equality of the entire object. Two objects that have the same fields but different reference are considered equal if all key-value pairs match. For primitive values like strings and numbers it works perfectly as a uniqueness guard.

items.question: What is the $type number for ObjectId?
items.answer: ObjectId has BSON type number 7. You can query it with { _id: { $type: 7 } } or { _id: { $type: 'objectId' } }. The string alias is always safer to read and recommend in code.

items.question: Can $inc create a field that doesn't exist?
items.answer: Yes. If the field does not exist, $inc creates it and sets it to the increment value. Example: { $inc: { views: 1 } } on a document without a views field creates { views: 1 }. This is useful for lazy initialization of counters.

items.question: [Medium] Why does MongoDB require explicit $and when the same field appears twice in a filter?
items.answer: JavaScript objects cannot have duplicate keys — { age: { $gt: 18 }, age: { $lt: 60 } } silently overwrites the first condition, leaving only age < 60. To apply multiple conditions to the same field you must use explicit $and: { $and: [ { age: { $gt: 18 } }, { age: { $lt: 60 } } ] }. However the cleaner shorthand is to combine operators in one object: { age: { $gt: 18, $lt: 60 } } — MongoDB evaluates this as AND on the same field.

items.question: [Medium] What happens to $inc if the field value is a string instead of a number?
items.answer: MongoDB throws a WriteError — it cannot increment a non-numeric value. The operation fails and the document is not modified. To prevent this, ensure field types are enforced using Mongoose schema types or MongoDB schema validation. You can also check the current type first with a $type filter in the query: db.users.updateOne({ _id: id, views: { $type: 'number' } }, { $inc: { views: 1 } }).

items.question: [Medium] Can you use $regex on indexed fields and does it improve performance?
items.answer: A B-tree index helps $regex only when the pattern is anchored at the start with ^ — like /^Shiv/. This turns it into a range scan on the index similar to a prefix search. A non-anchored pattern like /shivam/ or a pattern anchored at the end like /kumar$/ cannot use the index and performs a full collection scan even if an index exists on the field. For these cases, a text index with $text is far more efficient.

items.question: [Medium] How do you search for documents where an array field contains exactly one specific value and nothing else?
items.answer: Combine $all and $size. $all ensures the array contains the required value and $size ensures the array length is exactly 1: db.users.find({ skills: { $all: ['Node.js'], $size: 1 } }). This returns only documents where skills is exactly ['Node.js'] — no more, no less. Without $size, $all would match arrays containing Node.js along with other values.

items.question: [Medium] What is the difference between $push with $each and calling $push multiple times?
items.answer: Calling $push multiple times in separate update calls requires multiple network round-trips to the database. Each call is a separate atomic operation. $push with $each inserts multiple elements in a SINGLE atomic operation and a single round-trip: { $push: { skills: { $each: ['TypeScript', 'Docker', 'AWS'] } } }. This is more efficient, reduces network overhead, and is fully atomic — all elements are added together or none are.

items.question: [Medium] How do you query nested object fields in MongoDB?
items.answer: Use dot notation to access nested fields in query filters. Example for a document with address: { city: 'Delhi', pinCode: '110001' } — query with db.users.find({ 'address.city': 'Delhi' }). You can nest as deep as needed: db.users.find({ 'address.location.coordinates.lat': 28.6 }). In Mongoose, dot notation works the same way in filter objects. Always wrap the dot-notation path in quotes in the query object.

items.question: [Medium] What is the difference between find().sort().skip().limit() order and why does order matter?
items.answer: MongoDB processes query modifiers in a fixed logical order regardless of how you chain them in code: (1) filter, (2) sort, (3) skip, (4) limit. The chaining order in your JavaScript code does not change execution order — find().limit(10).skip(20).sort({age:-1}) is identical to find().sort({age:-1}).skip(20).limit(10). However, always write sort before skip and limit in code for readability and to avoid confusion. Most importantly, ALWAYS sort before paginating or you will get inconsistent page results.

items.question: [Medium] Can $currentDate be used to set both a Date and a Timestamp in one update?
items.answer: Yes. $currentDate accepts a map of fields to type specifications. { $currentDate: { lastLogin: true, lastLoginTs: { $type: 'timestamp' } } } sets lastLogin as a BSON Date (millisecond precision, human-readable) and lastLoginTs as a BSON Timestamp (used internally for replication, not recommended for application logic). For application timestamps, always use Date type (true or { $type: 'date' }).

items.question: [Advanced] How would you implement a 'find documents where any element in an array of objects has a field matching a regex' query?
items.answer: Use $elemMatch combined with $regex: db.users.find({ contacts: { $elemMatch: { email: { $regex: /@gmail\.com$/i } } } }). This finds users who have at least one contact with a Gmail address. Without $elemMatch, dot notation db.users.find({ 'contacts.email': { $regex: /@gmail/ } }) also works for a single condition per element but $elemMatch is required when multiple conditions must be satisfied by the same array element simultaneously.

items.question: [Advanced] How does MongoDB's $nor behave when a field is completely absent from a document?
items.answer: $nor: [{ role: 'guest' }] matches documents where role is NOT 'guest'. This includes documents where the role field does not exist at all, because a missing field does not equal 'guest'. This is a common subtle bug — $nor can accidentally match documents that are simply missing the field. To be safe, combine with $exists: { $nor: [{ role: 'guest' }, { role: { $exists: false } }] } to exclude both guests and documents with no role field.

items.question: [Advanced] How would you use arrayFilters with $[identifier] to update all matching elements in an array?
items.answer: The positional $ operator updates only the FIRST matching element. To update ALL elements matching a condition, use the filtered positional operator $[identifier] with the arrayFilters option. Example — mark all pending items in an order as shipped: db.orders.updateOne({ _id: orderId }, { $set: { 'items.$[item].status': 'shipped' } }, { arrayFilters: [{ 'item.status': 'pending' }] }). The identifier 'item' in $[item] is arbitrary and matches the identifier in arrayFilters. This updates EVERY items element where status is 'pending' in one atomic operation.

items.question: [Advanced] How do comparison operators behave when the field is missing vs null vs zero vs false?
items.answer: MongoDB has specific BSON comparison order for mixed types. Missing field: $gt, $lt comparisons on non-existent fields return no match — the document is excluded. Null: null is less than any number, string, or boolean in BSON sort order. Zero: 0 is a number and compares normally. False: false is a boolean, treated as less than true. Practically: { age: { $gt: 0 } } will NOT match documents where age is null or missing. To include null/missing fields, combine with $or: { $or: [ { age: { $gt: 0 } }, { age: null } ] }.

items.question: [Advanced] What is the most efficient way to implement a search that must match across multiple fields with different operators?
items.answer: Combine indexing strategy with query design. Step 1 — create a compound index on the most selective fields: db.users.createIndex({ isActive: 1, role: 1, age: 1 }). Step 2 — structure your query to use the index prefix from left to right (equality fields first, then range fields last): db.users.find({ isActive: true, role: { $in: ['admin','manager'] }, age: { $gte: 25 } }). Step 3 — use .explain('executionStats') to verify the query uses IXSCAN (index scan) not COLLSCAN (collection scan). The rule is: equality filters first, then $in, then range operators ($gt, $lt) last for optimal index utilization.

items: BSON types: String, Number, Boolean, Date, ObjectId, Array, Object, Null, Decimal128, Binary.
Comparison: $eq $ne $gt $gte $lt $lte $in $nin — compare field to a value.
$and is implicit when listing multiple fields; use explicit $and when same field appears twice.
Element: $exists checks field presence, $type checks the BSON data type of a field.
Evaluation: $regex for patterns, $text for full-text search, $expr to compare two fields.
Array query: $all (must contain all), $size (exact length), $elemMatch (element-level conditions).
Update arrays: $push (add), $pull (remove by value), $addToSet (add if unique), $pop (remove by position).
Never update without $set or you will replace the entire document.
Use $addToSet over $push when array should not have duplicates.
Use $text over $regex for keyword search on large collections — it uses an index.
